iew0q1.A: Correct. IPO = Initial Public Offering — the first sale of a company's shares to the public, turning a private company into a listed one.
iew0q1.B: Invented term. Profit optimisation is an internal finance activity and has no standard 'IPO' abbreviation.
iew0q1.C: Invented term. No such standard business abbreviation exists.
iew0q1.D: Invented term. A portfolio overview is an investor's report, not a company event.

iew0q2.A: That is a sole proprietorship — one owner, no separate legal identity.
iew0q2.B: Correct. A partnership is two or more people sharing ownership, profits, liabilities and responsibilities.
iew0q2.C: That is a public sector undertaking or state-owned enterprise, not a partnership.
iew0q2.D: Every partnership rests on an ownership agreement; 'no formal structure' describes an informal arrangement, not a legal form.

iew0q3.A: Market trend analysis is a research activity that uses data, not the creative techniques listed.
iew0q3.B: Correct. Problem-solving, critical thinking and idea generation are the standard toolkit for enhancing creativity and innovation.
iew0q3.C: Brand awareness is a marketing outcome, built through communication rather than ideation techniques.
iew0q3.D: Streamlining production is an operations and process-efficiency concern.

iew0q4.A: 'Treat' is a near-miss spelling designed to catch a rushed reader.
iew0q4.B: Correct. SWOT = Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats. Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external.
iew0q4.D: Tactics are what you do after the analysis, not a quadrant of it.

iew0q5.A: A sole proprietorship is a legal business structure — one owner.
iew0q5.B: A partnership is a legal business structure — shared ownership.
iew0q5.C: A corporation is a legal business structure — a separate legal entity.
iew0q5.D: Correct. A trademark is a form of intellectual property protecting a brand name or mark. It says nothing about how the business is owned.

iew0q6.A: Close but wrong expansion — a KPI measures performance against a goal, not a process step.
iew0q6.B: Correct. KPI = Key Performance Indicator, a measurable value showing how effectively an objective is being met.
iew0q6.C: Invented expansion. Productivity and knowledge are things a KPI might measure, not what the letters stand for.
iew0q6.D: Invented term. Profit is one possible KPI, not what the letters mean.

iew0q7.A: True but incomplete — a target market alone does not start a business.
iew0q7.B: True but incomplete — a plan without a market or funding goes nowhere.
iew0q7.C: True but incomplete — funding without a market or plan is the classic failure mode the course warns about.
iew0q7.D: Correct. All three are necessary together; each option alone is insufficient.

iew0q8.A: Reducing quality is a harm, never a benefit.
iew0q8.B: Correct. Social media's distinctive value is a direct two-way channel to customers, which builds engagement and brand loyalty.
iew0q8.C: Social media complements a website; it does not replace the channel you own.
iew0q8.D: Restricting feedback destroys the main advantage of the channel.

iew0q9.A: Their models differ — OYO aggregates hotel rooms, Swiggy delivers food.
iew0q9.B: Both are tech-enabled, but this is true of thousands of companies and is not what links these two specifically.
iew0q9.C: Correct. Both crossed the $1 billion valuation mark, making them unicorns — the shared trait the question is testing.
iew0q9.D: No business model is free from financial risk; both have absorbed heavy losses.

iew0q10.A: Copying is imitation, the opposite of the value-creating activity entrepreneurship describes.
iew0q10.B: Correct. Of the options offered, starting and running a business venture is the definition of entrepreneurship.
iew0q10.C: That describes research and academic work, which may precede a venture but is not entrepreneurship.
iew0q10.D: Profit is a possible outcome, not the activity itself.

iew1q1.A: Avoiding collaboration removes the very feedback that turns a failure into a lesson.
iew1q1.B: Correct. The course treats failure as data: the lessons and insights you extract are what make the attempt worth something.
iew1q1.C: Jumping away immediately means the learning is never captured.
iew1q1.D: Blaming external factors blocks the honest analysis that produces the lesson.

iew1q2.A: Cost-versus-quality balance matters operationally but is not the characteristic the course names for success.
iew1q2.B: Ignoring customer feedback is the behaviour the entire course argues against.
iew1q2.C: Correct. Strategic planning plus adaptability to market change is the pairing the course identifies — plan, then adjust as evidence arrives.
iew1q2.D: 'Solely' on profit ignores customers and market fit, the stated causes of failure.

iew1q3.A: Correct. The purpose of selling is to identify a real customer and market need and fulfil it — everything else follows from that.
iew1q3.B: Aggressive pricing is a tactic, and profit maximisation is an outcome, not the objective of the exchange.
iew1q3.C: Promotion communicates value; it does not create the need the product serves.
iew1q3.D: Discounting is a sales lever, not the reason the product exists.

iew1q4.A: Maintaining the status quo is the opposite of disruption.
iew1q4.B: Imitation competes inside existing norms rather than challenging them.
iew1q4.C: Correct. A disruptive idea changes the rules of the market — it challenges existing norms rather than competing on them.
iew1q4.D: Strict adherence to standards is conventional, not disruptive.

iew1q5.A: 'Without innovation' removes the mechanism by which entrepreneurship creates new value.
iew1q5.B: Customer validation is a method inside entrepreneurship, not how it drives an economy.
iew1q5.C: Correct. Entrepreneurs grow an economy by identifying real market problems and solving them, which creates value, jobs and new markets.
iew1q5.D: Market isolation avoids the competition that drives productivity.

iew1q6.A: Degrees are explicitly not a prerequisite — the course makes this point directly.
iew1q6.B: Rigid execution of the original plan is what Lean Startup replaces.
iew1q6.C: Lean Startup is about validated learning, not financial optimisation.
iew1q6.D: Correct. The method's core is continuous learning validated by customer feedback, through Build–Measure–Learn.

iew1q7.A: Correct. The two objectives are validating the customer and developing iteratively, so each version is tested against evidence.
iew1q7.B: Company building without market analysis is the premature-scaling failure Lean Startup exists to prevent.
iew1q7.C: Rapid scaling before product–market fit is the opposite of the method.
iew1q7.D: Agile engineering is one of the three components, but 'without customer feedback' removes the point of it.

iew1q8.A: Correct. Institutions add value by bridging academic research to real market applications — this is the stated mission of centres like GDC.
iew1q8.B: Exclusively theoretical research never reaches the market.
iew1q8.C: Isolation from the marketplace removes the translation step entirely.

iew1q9.A: Correct. Validated learning through continuous experimentation and data is a core part of the definition.
iew1q9.B: Correct. Build–Measure–Learn is the cycle that operationalises it.
iew1q9.C: Correct. Deciding on empirical evidence rather than assumption is the defining shift.
iew1q9.D: Correct. Regular customer engagement is how the evidence is gathered. All four describe the same practice — this is a select-all question where every option is right.

iew1q10.A: Adopting Lean Startup is the remedy the course prescribes, not a mistake.
iew1q10.B: Correct. Over-focusing on the product while neglecting the market is the classic founder error.
iew1q10.C: Correct. Building a solution without engaging potential customers is the other classic error — it produces a product nobody needs.
iew1q10.D: Writing a business plan and sizing the market is sound practice, not a mistake.

iew2q1.A: Correct. 'No market need' is the single most common cause of startup failure in the post-mortem analysis the course cites.
iew2q1.B: A skilled team is an asset; its absence is a cause of failure, not its presence.
iew2q1.C: Sufficient funding helps — and the course notes money alone never saves a startup, but it is not a cause of failure.
iew2q1.D: A user-friendly product is a strength.

iew2q2.A: Individual achievement can pull a team apart when it is not tied to a common goal.
iew2q2.B: Lack of diversity narrows the perspectives available; the course argues diverse teams perform better.
iew2q2.C: Frequent disagreement corrodes unity rather than creating it.
iew2q2.D: Correct. A shared vision and common ideology is what holds a founding team together through a long, uncertain journey.

iew2q3.A: Entering the market without validation is the behaviour the course warns against.
iew2q3.B: Correct. Founders launch to learn: iterate the product while learning from customers.
iew2q3.C: Long-term planning without short-term feedback removes the evidence loop.
iew2q3.D: Internal team building matters, but exploring the market is what a launch is for.

iew2q4.A: True — direct feedback on the product is one contribution.
iew2q4.B: True — uncovering pain points and preferences is another.
iew2q4.C: True — validating assumptions is the third.
iew2q4.D: Correct. All three are genuine contributions of customer interaction, so the catch-all is right.

iew2q5.A: Broad marketing comes later; early adopters are too few to be a distribution channel.
iew2q5.B: Correct. Early adopters matter because they give critical feedback that refines the product while it can still change cheaply.
iew2q5.C: Production capacity is an operations concern, not something customers expand.
iew2q5.D: Early adopters buy the product; they are not a funding source.

iew2q6.A: Correct. 'Funding guarantees success' is the named misconception — the course states money is not why startups die, product–market fit is.
iew2q6.B: Scaling the team strategically is sound practice.
iew2q6.C: Prioritising customer needs is exactly what the course recommends.
iew2q6.D: Team-building is useful; the trap option is the funding one.

iew2q7.A: The founder's belief drives the venture but cannot validate it — that is the inventor-syndrome trap.
iew2q7.B: Investors validate the business case, not whether the product solves a real need.
iew2q7.C: Correct. Only customers validate a product, by using it and paying for it.
iew2q7.D: Marketing teams communicate value; they do not confirm it exists.

iew2q8.A: Correct. Stagnation is a signal to re-examine the strategy and pivot if the evidence says the current path is not working.
iew2q8.B: Spending more on marketing a product nobody needs amplifies the problem.
iew2q8.C: Ignoring it wastes the remaining runway.
iew2q8.D: Cost-cutting extends runway but does not address why progress stalled.

iew2q9.A: Correct. Strong leadership and a clear vision are essential for the long haul.
iew2q9.B: Correct. Effective communication and collaboration keep a diverse team functioning.
iew2q9.C: Ignoring customer feedback contradicts the central lesson of the course.
iew2q9.D: Limited market research plus an advertising focus is the failure pattern, not a success characteristic.

iew2q10.A: Correct. Conviction in the vision is what carries founders through the long uncertain stretch — the course's 'be bold and be perseverant'.
iew2q10.B: Chasing endless funding is the misconception the course calls out.
iew2q10.C: Speed of development is useful but not the essential founder quality.
iew2q10.D: Programming skill is a role-specific ability, not a founder requirement.

iew3q1.A: Aesthetics are a styling outcome; empathy operates at the level of understanding needs.
iew3q1.B: Cost reduction comes from engineering and manufacturing choices.
iew3q1.C: Empathy is directed at users, not at rival designers.
iew3q1.D: Correct. Empathy is what makes design user-centred — it is why the Vein Tracer began with hospital visits and no product in mind.

iew3q2.A: Correct. A varied skill set and diverse perspectives is what the course prescribes — different disciplines, backgrounds, even languages.
iew3q2.B: A single domain expertise leaves blind spots across the rest of the problem.
iew3q2.C: Limited experience and poor collaboration are weaknesses, not criteria.
iew3q2.D: Homogeneous teams reproduce the same assumptions.

iew3q3.A: Correct. Thinking in product categories gives you Plan B, C and D — it diversifies risk and keeps you adaptable if one product fails.
iew3q3.B: Cost-cutting is unrelated to the category-versus-product choice.
iew3q3.C: The category approach widens customer engagement rather than reducing it.
iew3q3.D: It expands market exploration; the single-product approach is what narrows it.

iew3q4.A: True — flexibility and willingness to adapt is one of the named qualities.
iew3q4.B: True — lowering ego and collaborating is explicitly advised.
iew3q4.C: True — taking a defined role is the third.
iew3q4.D: Correct. All three are named together in the team-building session.

iew3q5.A: Correct. A design brief, or need statement, is built from the functional requirement plus the user requirement.
iew3q5.B: Budget and audience are project context, not the core of the brief.
iew3q5.C: Timeline and brand vision are management and marketing inputs.
iew3q5.D: Full technical specifications come later; the brief defines what is needed, not how to build it.

iew3q6.A: Correct. Collaborative design pools resources and integrates expertise from different disciplines — 'without collaboration, innovation cannot move forward'.
iew3q6.B: Manufacturing efficiency is a production concern.
iew3q6.C: Aesthetic appeal is one possible output, not the reason to collaborate.
iew3q6.D: Administrative simplification is not a design outcome.

iew3q7.A: Regulation adds administrative work rather than simplifying it.
iew3q7.B: Regulation constrains innovation to safe forms; it does not make it unrestricted.
iew3q7.C: Correct. Regulatory barriers exist to protect public health and ensure legal compliance — and as a side effect they deter new entrants, which can protect your position.
iew3q7.D: Regulation formalises the market, the opposite of informal practice.

iew3q8.A: A solution inside the problem statement closes off the exploration before it starts.
iew3q8.B: Correct. The essential element is defining the problem clearly — the course reframes vague statements into specific ones before solving.
iew3q8.C: A budget is a project constraint, not part of the problem definition.
iew3q8.D: Leading with team capability biases the problem toward what you can already do.

iew3q9.A: Strict procedural compliance suppresses the experimentation innovation needs.
iew3q9.B: Internal competition fragments the knowledge sharing that innovation depends on.
iew3q9.C: Correct. Interdisciplinary collaboration is the crucial factor — innovation comes from combining perspectives across fields.
iew3q9.D: Money helps but does not generate innovation by itself.

iew3q10.A: Correct. Prior art is the term for previously granted patents and published applications, searched to establish novelty and non-obviousness.
iew3q10.B: A generic phrase with no standing in patent law.
iew3q10.C: Past literature is broader and not the patent-specific term.
iew3q10.D: Invented term with no standing in patent law — it sounds official, which is the whole trap.

iew4q1.A: Addressing pain points effectively is what prevents failure.
iew4q1.B: Prioritising customer satisfaction is protective, not a cause of failure.
iew4q1.C: Correct. An innovative product still fails when the team has not understood what customers actually need — innovation does not substitute for understanding.
iew4q1.D: Regular feedback is the safeguard against this exact failure.

iew4q2.A: Correct. Outside-in thinking starts from outside the company — the customer's requirements — and works inward to the product.
iew4q2.B: Improving internal processes is inside-out thinking.
iew4q2.C: Over-engineering is what happens when the technical team leads instead of the customer.
iew4q2.D: Disregarding feedback is the opposite of taking an outside-in view.

iew4q3.A: Scaling quickly is a later-stage problem, and premature scaling is a mistake rather than an early challenge.
iew4q3.B: Correct. Assembling a skilled, cohesive team is the hard early-stage problem — the course puts team before idea.
iew4q3.C: Venture capital is not easily acquired early; the wording makes this false.
iew4q3.D: Marketing strategy becomes pressing once you have a product and a validated market.

iew4q4.A: Urban-targeted social media misses the rural audience entirely.
iew4q4.B: Correct. Government schemes already reach rural households and carry the trust and distribution a startup cannot build alone.
iew4q4.C: Digital platforms assume connectivity and digital habits that may not be present.
iew4q4.D: Door-to-door selling in urban regions targets the wrong geography.

iew4q5.A: Correct. Partnerships and influential figures lend reach and credibility.
iew4q5.B: 'Solely relying' on MLM and digital ads is the exclusionary option — the word 'solely' makes it wrong.
iew4q5.C: Correct. Interactive demonstrations let people experience an unfamiliar product.
iew4q5.D: Correct. Building and educating communities creates durable awareness.

iew4q6.A: True — cutting intermediaries lowers the final price.
iew4q6.B: True — subsidies for eco-friendly products improve affordability.
iew4q6.C: True — bulk institutional orders improve unit economics.
iew4q6.D: Correct. All three pricing levers were used in the solar oven case.

iew4q7.A: Correct. Investors back evidence of a real, solvable problem — the course frames this as the first thing to demonstrate.
iew4q7.B: Ignoring competition signals that the market has not been studied.
iew4q7.C: 'Solely futuristic technology' with no present problem is exactly what investors avoid.
iew4q7.D: Vague or exaggerated claims destroy credibility.

iew4q8.A: Correct. A new market has its own cultural and economic conditions, and understanding them comes before entering.
iew4q8.B: Skipping research and going on instinct is the failure mode.
iew4q8.C: Ignoring local regulation invites legal and compliance failure.
iew4q8.D: Unadapted products are the standard way foreign entrants fail.

iew4q9.A: Ignoring the problem is the unaware end of the scale.
iew4q9.B: Correct. An urgent or active problem means the person recognises it and is already searching for a solution — the best customers to approach.
iew4q9.C: Recognising but refusing to act is passive, not active.
iew4q9.D: Adjusting without solving is coping, which signals the need is not urgent.

iew4q10.A: No awareness at all is the stage below passive.
iew4q10.B: Correct. Passive means the person knows the problem exists but has no motivation to change — aware, but not moving.
iew4q10.C: Motivation without understanding is not what passive describes.
iew4q10.D: Being unable to act is a capability constraint; passive is about missing motivation, not ability. This is the distractor most people pick.

iew5q1.A: Obstacles block translation; the question asks what enables it.
iew5q1.B: Correct. Industry partnership is the bridge that turns lab research into products society actually uses — the core argument of the R.E.INV.ENT model.
iew5q1.C: Confidentiality has a role in patenting, but keeping results closed prevents societal benefit.
iew5q1.D: Rivalry with industry removes the collaboration the translation depends on.

iew5q2.A: High margins would attract investors, not repel them.
iew5q2.B: Correct. Medical devices have poor success rates — long development, clinical trials and certification mean most never reach market, which makes investors wary.
iew5q2.C: Growing demand is a reason to invest.
iew5q2.D: Medical device R&D cycles are long, not short; the statement is false as well as unpersuasive.

iew5q3.A: Correct. Everything starts with identifying the problem and understanding the functional requirements — 'need to have, not nice to have'.
iew5q3.B: Marketing comes after there is something worth marketing.
iew5q3.C: Training and resourcing are execution concerns, not the first design step.
iew5q3.D: IPR matters, but it protects a solution you have already defined.

iew5q4.A: Telemedicine lowered cost and extended reach; the claim is simply false.
iew5q4.B: Correct. By handling consultations remotely it reduced the load on physical facilities when they were overwhelmed.
iew5q4.C: It removed access barriers rather than creating them.
iew5q4.D: It simplified delivery for routine care.

iew5q5.A: Marketing content is not what a pilot run produces.
iew5q5.B: Correct. Pilot production exists to test the design in realistic conditions and adapt features based on user feedback before committing to mass production.
iew5q5.C: Patents should already be filed before this stage.
iew5q5.D: Controlled lab research happens earlier, at proof-of-concept.

iew5q6.A: At idea conception there is often nothing specific enough to patent.
iew5q6.B: A working prototype is a reasonable moment, but the binding deadline is commercialisation.
iew5q6.C: Correct. Secure IPR before commercialising — once the product is public, disclosure can destroy novelty and the right to patent.
iew5q6.D: By the time it is widely available, protection is likely lost.

iew5q7.A: Start-ups can license, but so can others — 'only' makes this wrong.
iew5q7.B: Industry can license, but again not exclusively.
iew5q7.C: NGOs can license, including for non-profit deployment.
iew5q7.D: Correct. Start-ups, industry and NGOs are all eligible licensees; technology licensing is not restricted to one kind of body.

iew5q8.A: Correct. TRL = Technology Readiness Levels, the 1–9 scale running from concept through proof-of-concept, prototype and product to market.
iew5q8.B: Invented expansion. 'Research limits' has nothing to do with measuring how close a technology is to deployment.
iew5q8.C: Invented expansion — plausible-sounding, which is the trap.
iew5q8.D: Invented expansion. Testing and reliability are activities within development, not the name of the 1-9 maturity scale.

iew5q9.A: Correct. A PoC exists to show the concept actually works — functional feasibility. It is not expected to be scalable, pretty or finished.
iew5q9.B: Industrial scalability belongs to the later product and pilot stages.
iew5q9.C: Patents may follow, but they are not what a PoC demonstrates.
iew5q9.D: Ideas without implementation are not a proof of anything.

iew5q10.A: Correct. Functional requirements come from the people who will use and be affected by the product, so thorough stakeholder interviews are the best practice.
iew5q10.B: Relying on assumptions instead of users is the failure mode the course warns about.
iew5q10.C: Developer convenience optimises the wrong thing.
iew5q10.D: Ignoring scope and timeline produces requirements nobody can deliver.

iew6q1.A: Lean methods are useful tools but they are not what makes an approach human-centred.
iew6q1.B: Correct. Human-centred work rests on building empathy and doing real user research before deciding anything.
iew6q1.C: Traditional marketing pushes a message outward rather than learning from users.
iew6q1.D: 'Solely on product ideas' is exactly the inward focus human-centred design corrects.

iew6q2.A: Correct. Iterative testing and feedback loops are how you find out whether the product actually matches what customers expect.
iew6q2.B: Aesthetics over functionality inverts the priority.
iew6q2.D: Skipping prototyping removes the cheapest way to test expectations.

iew6q3.A: Correct. Together they connect day-to-day business operations with innovation — design stops being decoration and becomes a strategic function.
iew6q3.B: Mock-ups are an output of the process, not its organisational benefit.
iew6q3.C: 'Only' creative ideas understates what strategic planning and research contribute.
iew6q3.D: Quick decisions without research is the opposite of what these disciplines provide.

iew6q4.A: 'Solely' the core idea ignores feasibility and the business.
iew6q4.B: Correct. The designer's job is to balance all three: what users need, what technology permits, and what the business requires.
iew6q4.C: Letting customer experience override business goals breaks the balance in the other direction.
iew6q4.D: Prioritising feasibility over desirability produces something buildable that nobody wants.

iew6q5.A: Complex, detailed questions confuse people and shut them down.
iew6q5.B: Opening on a secondary objective wastes the interviewee's attention.
iew6q5.C: Correct. People share honestly once they trust you — build rapport first, then probe at the right moment.
iew6q5.D: A rigid formal structure prevents the unexpected disclosures that make interviews valuable.

iew6q6.A: Technical specifications and timelines belong to the project plan, not the brief.
iew6q6.B: Marketing strategy is downstream of the design brief.
iew6q6.D: Correct. A robust brief identifies user pain points, maps the user journey and ensures the solution fits the user's wider ecosystem.

iew6q7.A: Lateral thinking is a creativity technique, not a management discipline.
iew6q7.B: Overseeing teams and timelines is project management.
iew6q7.C: Stakeholder collaboration is part of it but does not define it.
iew6q7.D: Correct. Design management is a structured process for achieving business objectives through design.

iew6q8.A: High fees are a client cost, never a thing clients seek.
iew6q8.B: Correct. Quality, speed and transparency are the three named in the enterprise UX session.
iew6q8.C: Extended timelines are a drawback, not a quality sought.
iew6q8.D: Minimal interaction is the opposite of the collaboration clients want.

iew6q9.A: Timeline and budget are planning artefacts.
iew6q9.B: Competitor benchmarking informs strategy but is not the brief's core.
iew6q9.C: Correct. Specific user personas and their pain points are what make a brief actionable for designers.
iew6q9.D: Finalised marketing plans come after the product is defined.

iew6q10.A: Marketing success is a downstream result, not why empathy for both sides matters.
iew6q10.B: Prioritising aesthetics is not a balance at all.
iew6q10.C: Correct. Holding both perspectives keeps creative ideas tethered to objectives that the business can realistically meet.
iew6q10.D: Empathy for two constituencies adds complexity rather than reducing it.

iew7q1.A: Economic stability is a condition, not an approach to innovation.
iew7q1.B: Correct. Design thinking is defined by collaboration, iteration and a non-linear process — the 'squiggly line'.
iew7q1.D: Short-term focus works against the iteration design thinking requires.

iew7q2.A: Brainstorming generates volume but does not specifically work by linking unrelated domains.
iew7q2.B: Correct. Synectics is the method built on analogy — direct, personal, symbolic and fantasy — to connect unrelated concepts.
iew7q2.C: Mind mapping organises ideas you already have.
iew7q2.D: SWOT is a strategic analysis tool, not an ideation method.

iew7q3.A: Correct. Market need, technical feasibility and business viability — the same three lenses as desirability, feasibility and viability.
iew7q3.B: Advertising, packaging and distribution are go-to-market details.
iew7q3.C: Plausible-sounding but not the triad taught.
iew7q3.D: Profit and headcount are outcomes and resources, not the decision factors.

iew7q4.A: Correct. The Business Model Canvas puts the whole model on one page as a visual, which is why it works as a communication tool for investors and mentors.
iew7q4.B: A balance sheet shows financial position, not the business model.
iew7q4.C: A P&L shows performance over a period.
iew7q4.D: An org chart shows reporting lines.

iew7q5.A: Scaling before measuring is premature scaling.
iew7q5.B: Patents are a parallel legal track, not a stage of the loop.
iew7q5.C: Correct. Build → Measure → Learn: after building the MVP you measure customer response and learn from it.
iew7q5.D: Financial statements are not part of the cycle.

iew7q6.A: True — collaboration gives access to resources you could not afford alone.
iew7q6.C: True — it creates a community of peers.
iew7q6.D: Correct. All three benefits are named together.

iew7q7.A: Correct. Fractional ownership splits a high-value physical asset among many owners — NetJets selling shares of private jets.
iew7q7.B: Digital goods can be copied infinitely, so there is no scarcity to divide.
iew7q7.C: IP licensing is a different model.
iew7q7.D: Leasing transfers use for a period without transferring any ownership share.

iew7q8.A: High investment, large workforce and expensive marketing are costs, not criteria for success.
iew7q8.B: Correct. A clear value proposition, scalability and sustainable revenue streams are what make a model work.
iew7q8.C: 'Minimal effort' is wishful rather than a criterion.
iew7q8.D: A single revenue source and a limited market are fragilities.

iew7q9.A: Correct. Revenue growth, customer acquisition and customer retention are the three metric families the course names.
iew7q9.B: Useful operational measures, but not the headline set for business success.
iew7q9.C: Brand and social reach are vanity-adjacent and indirect.
iew7q9.D: Mixes one real metric with spend and aesthetics.

iew7q10.A: Lean Canvas is not a fundraising instrument.
iew7q10.B: A five-year financial plan is the opposite of lean — too speculative to be useful early.
iew7q10.C: Correct. Its value is speed: it lets you lay out and test business-model assumptions quickly, one customer segment at a time.
iew7q10.D: Organisational structure is not what the canvas describes.

iew8q1.A: Early adopters create advantage, not disadvantage.
iew8q1.B: Correct. They validate that real demand exists, early enough that the feedback can still change the product cheaply.
iew8q1.C: Early adopters typically accelerate first revenue.
iew8q1.D: Marketing effort is not the point of identifying them.

iew8q2.A: True — an entrepreneurial mindset is the first named trait.
iew8q2.B: True — adaptability and resilience carry founders through pivots.
iew8q2.C: True — ethics and values are explicitly included.
iew8q2.D: Correct. All three are named together as the characteristics to develop.

iew8q3.A: Operational detail is not what an investor pitch turns on.
iew8q3.B: Correct. Investors need to see a model that scales and makes money — the reviewers put it bluntly: any VC wants to know how they will make money.
iew8q3.C: Market size is one supporting slide, not the essential element.
iew8q3.D: Industry trends are context, not the business case.

iew8q4.A: An MVP exists precisely to validate, so 'without validation' contradicts it.
iew8q4.B: Correct. The MVP attracts early-adopter customers and validates the product idea with the smallest feature set that can be used.
iew8q4.C: Short-term revenue is not its purpose.
iew8q4.D: An MVP deliberately sacrifices polish for learning speed.

iew8q5.A: True — identifying target customers and users comes first.
iew8q5.B: True — listing their top three problems is the next step.
iew8q5.C: True — developing a solution for each problem follows.
iew8q5.D: Correct. All three are the opening steps of a Lean Canvas, done in that order.

iew8q6.A: Correct. Competitiveness is sustained by continuous improvement and innovation — Atomberg's position came from exactly this.
iew8q6.B: Raising prices incrementally does not make a product more competitive.

iew8q7.A: Physical property covers tangible assets like land and equipment.
iew8q7.B: Correct. Intellectual property is the legal protection for creations of the mind — it prevents unauthorised use of original works.
iew8q7.C: 'Commercial asset' is a generic accounting phrase.
iew8q7.D: Industrial design is one specific type of IP, not the umbrella term.

iew8q8.B: Correct. The four IPR types are patents, copyrights, trademarks and trade secrets.

iew8q9.A: Correct. Customer acquisition is about bringing in new customers efficiently and at sustainable cost — the cost per acquisition is what matters.
iew8q9.B: Maximising short-term revenue can mean acquiring customers at a loss.
iew8q9.C: Ignoring feedback undermines retention and therefore acquisition economics.
iew8q9.D: Word of mouth alone is not a strategy you can control or scale.

iew8q10.A: Correct. A strong UVP states clearly how you meet customer needs better than the alternatives, which is what attracts customers and keeps them.
iew8q10.B: 'Solely' financial metrics with no customer consideration is not a value proposition.
iew8q10.C: Infrastructure over customer needs inverts the priority.
iew8q10.D: Cutting quality to cut price weakens the proposition rather than sharpening it.

iew9q1.A: True — self-doubt about your own skills is one of the named barriers.
iew9q1.B: True — fear of negative feedback stops people showing the idea to anyone.
iew9q1.C: True — funding difficulty is the third.
iew9q1.D: Correct. All three barriers sit between having an idea and acting on it.

iew9q2.A: Funders matter, but the course is explicit that money is not what determines survival.
iew9q2.B: Correct. The target customer is the relationship that decides whether the startup lives — customers validate, pay and tell you what to build next.
iew9q2.C: Infrastructure is a resource, not a relationship.
iew9q2.D: Market needs are a thing you study, not a relationship you manage.

iew9q3.A: Correct. Government grants are the first risk capital available to early ventures and expect no return.
iew9q3.B: Correct. Seed funding and crowdfunding are the other typical early sources.
iew9q3.C: High-interest long-term loans are inappropriate for a pre-revenue startup with no cash flow to service them.
iew9q3.D: Equity funds come later, once the business is scalable enough for an investor to model an exit.

iew9q4.A: True — when education is aimed solely at getting a job, few graduates attempt ventures.
iew9q4.B: True — resource abundance can remove the pressure that drives innovation.
iew9q4.C: True — discouraging policy suppresses new venture formation.
iew9q4.D: Correct. All three explain why some regions lag.

iew9q5.A: Correct. Incubation is where the idea becomes a business: build the plan, secure resources, register the company, move prototype toward viable product.
iew9q5.B: Taking an idea to industry through IP or technology transfer is commercialisation, a different path.
iew9q5.C: Advanced R&D belongs to the research stage before incubation.
iew9q5.D: Scaling for global markets is the accelerator stage, after incubation.

iew9q6.A: Too harsh on both — it reduces entrepreneurs to profit-seekers and strips innovators of any goal.
iew9q6.B: Correct. The difference is framing: an entrepreneur sees a problem as a business opportunity, while an innovator is satisfied by solving it.
iew9q6.C: Working alone versus in teams is not the distinction; both do both.
iew9q6.D: Formal education is not required of either.

iew9q7.A: Administrative training is not why an engineer sits in a hospital.
iew9q7.B: Correct. Clinical immersion means observing diagnosis, treatment and follow-up with consent, to find unmet needs you would never learn about from outside.
iew9q7.D: Financial planning is unrelated to being present in the clinic.

iew9q8.A: Correct. Execution improves when you know precisely whose need you are meeting and what gap exists in the market.
iew9q8.B: Advertising cannot rescue an idea aimed at an undefined need.
iew9q8.C: Office infrastructure is irrelevant to execution quality.
iew9q8.D: Rigid adherence to the original plan prevents the pivots evidence demands.

iew9q9.A: Entrepreneurship is owning and building the venture yourself — the other path.
iew9q9.B: Correct. Commercialisation is handing the idea to industry via intellectual property or technology transfer.
iew9q9.C: Enterprise development is a general term for growing businesses.
iew9q9.D: Incubation is support given to a startup you are building yourself.

iew9q10.A: Correct. The Idea Generation stage is where the startup idea is first created and developed — germination, before any prototype exists.
iew9q10.B: Research investigates feasibility after there is an idea to test.
iew9q10.C: Incubation turns an existing idea into a viable product.
iew9q10.D: Scaling is the last stage, where a proven business grows — not where the idea is first formed.

iew10q1.A: Fantasy analogy is wish-fulfilment that ignores physics — 'the spoon feeds the child itself'.
iew10q1.B: Correct. Personal analogy is imagining yourself as part of the problem or object: 'if I were the spoon in a child's hand'.
iew10q1.C: Symbolic analogy compresses the essence into a short, often paradoxical phrase.
iew10q1.D: There is no such thing as a 'CAD analogy' — it is an invented option.

iew10q2.A: Additive is real — building up with clay, plaster of Paris or rubber, and 3D printing as the machine version.
iew10q2.B: Subtractive is real — cutting away from a block of styrene, styrofoam or PU foam; CNC machining is the powered version.
iew10q2.C: Forming is real — reshaping a sheet without adding or removing material, as in vacuum forming.
iew10q2.D: Correct. Lateral thinking is an ideation technique, not a way of physically making a prototype. That is why it is the odd one out.

iew10q3.A: Correct. Ideation → Concept Generation → Prototyping → Testing → Market Launch. Ideas first, launch last, testing before launch.
iew10q3.B: Puts ideation after testing, which is impossible — you cannot test what has not been conceived.
iew10q3.C: Ends with ideation, after the product has already launched.
iew10q3.D: Launches before prototyping or testing, the worst possible order.

iew10q4.A: Abductive reasoning infers the most likely explanation for an observation.
iew10q4.B: Deductive reasoning goes the other way — from a general rule to a specific case.
iew10q4.C: Correct. Inductive reasoning builds a general conclusion out of specific observations, which is how user research produces insight.
iew10q4.D: Analytical reasoning is a broad label, not one of the three types named in the course.

iew10q5.A: Increasing costs is the opposite of frugality.
iew10q5.B: Correct. Frugal innovation minimises waste and uses resources efficiently, which lowers cost without lowering usefulness.
iew10q5.C: Aesthetics over function is unrelated to frugality.
iew10q5.D: Scaling without cost discipline is the opposite again.

iew10q6.A: Correct. A PoC validates that the idea is feasible and viable — that it can actually work — before resources go into building the real thing.
iew10q6.B: The final product comes much later, after prototyping and pilot production.
iew10q6.C: Funding may follow a successful PoC but is not its purpose.
iew10q6.D: Prototypes for user feedback are the next stage; a PoC proves the principle first.

iew10q7.A: Finalising for immediate release skips the learning prototyping exists for.
iew10q7.B: Correct. Prototyping builds models to test and improve design, functionality and usability — and it is a communication tool as much as a physical one.
iew10q7.C: Large-scale production units are manufacturing, not prototyping.
iew10q7.D: Prototyping is inherently iterative; avoiding iteration defeats it.

iew10q8.A: Correct. Synectics exists to break conventional thinking and widen exploration — 'put the watchman in your mind to sleep'.
iew10q8.B: Converging on one perfect solution is the opposite of what it does.
iew10q8.C: Quick consensus suppresses the divergence the method needs.
iew10q8.D: Detailed technical analysis refines ideas; Synectics generates them.

iew10q9.A: Mutual franchising is one mechanism mentioned, but it is not the general answer and does not cover distributed production.
iew10q9.B: Correct. Entrepreneurs collaborate by pooling resources and distributing production — pooled inventory, single bid with multiple suppliers, distributed manufacturing as with the Etikoppaka artisans.
iew10q9.C: Competing in the same segment is rivalry, not collaboration — and its presence is why the catch-all is wrong here.
iew10q9.D: This is the one question in the set where 'All of the above' is incorrect, because option C is not collaboration.

iew10q10.A: Correct. Prototypes surface design flaws while they are still cheap to fix — far cheaper than discovering them after deployment.
iew10q10.B: A prototype is explicitly not the final version; the course says to state that when showing one.
iew10q10.C: Prototyping supplements market research, it does not replace it.
iew10q10.D: Aesthetics without user input is the opposite of what prototyping tests.

iew11q1.A: Correct. Needs vary enormously between individuals with disabilities, so the design has to start from observing actual users — user-centred design.
iew11q1.B: Exclusivity narrows who the product can serve, the opposite of the goal.
iew11q1.C: Profit maximisation is a business objective, not a design approach.
iew11q1.D: Cost reduction matters but does not determine whether the product meets the need.

iew11q2.A: Awareness of digital alternatives is a communications activity, not a design aim.
iew11q2.B: Correct. The two aims are making the user independent and helping them integrate socially — dignity as well as function.
iew11q2.C: Redesigning existing products is a method, not the aim.
iew11q2.D: Exclusive and expensive solutions exclude the people assistive technology is for.

iew11q3.A: Trendy and common means undifferentiated — easily copied, quickly forgotten.
iew11q3.B: Correct. A product succeeds by being relevant (it meets a real need) and differentiated (it is distinguishable from alternatives).
iew11q3.C: Cheap and generic competes only on price, which is the weakest position.
iew11q3.D: Expensive and complex adds cost and friction without necessarily adding value.

iew11q4.A: Guaranteed returns are unrealistic and destroy credibility with any serious investor.
iew11q4.B: Correct. What persuades is a genuinely unique and differentiated offering — something that cannot simply be bought elsewhere.
iew11q4.C: A vague value proposition is the most common reason a pitch fails.
iew11q4.D: Low cost with limited functionality gives neither investors nor customers a reason to choose you.

iew11q5.A: Material choice has little to do with production time, and speed would not justify the risk.
iew11q5.B: Correct. In B2C, cheap materials come back as returns, warranty claims and servicing — the saving is more than cancelled out downstream.
iew11q5.D: They typically worsen appearance and feel, not improve it.

iew11q6.A: Strong loyalty and retention reduce risk.
iew11q6.B: Correct. Depending on a handful of corporate clients means losing one can take a large share of revenue — concentration risk.

iew11q7.A: Speed is an AI advantage, so this does not answer what human interaction contributes.
iew11q7.B: Correct. Direct human contact builds empathy and an understanding of individual needs that a model working from aggregate data does not reach.
iew11q7.C: Machine learning improvement is again an AI advantage.
iew11q7.D: Breadth of capability is not the point of comparison here.

iew11q8.A: Correct. Interactive games that involve physical movement and coordination develop cognitive, motor and analytical skills together.
iew11q8.B: 'Solely' aesthetic and trendy design delivers no developmental benefit.
iew11q8.C: Technology used purely for entertainment does not build skills.
iew11q8.D: Cost-efficiency over engagement loses the child's attention, and an unengaged child learns nothing.

iew11q9.A: Correct. Evidence-based development means knowing exactly who the customer is and then measuring whether the solution actually had the intended impact.
iew11q9.B: Brand recognition and competitor analysis are market activities, not evidence about your solution's effect.
iew11q9.C: Advertising budgets and technical specs are downstream decisions.
iew11q9.D: Packaging and pricing come after the solution is shown to work.

iew11q10.A: Cost reduction is not why alignment with customer needs matters.
iew11q10.B: Correct. A product matched to real needs produces satisfaction that lasts, and satisfied customers stay — loyalty is the long-term payoff.
iew11q10.C: Following trends exclusively ignores the actual customer.
iew11q10.D: Manufacturing simplicity is an internal benefit.

iew12q1.A: Early identification narrows focus usefully; it does not cause unhealthy fixation.
iew12q1.B: Correct. A clearly identified problem gives the whole development effort a defined direction, so the team is not designing in the dark.
iew12q1.C: Nothing about early identification assumes problems are static — you revisit them as evidence arrives.
iew12q1.D: Identifying the problem properly requires user insight rather than overlooking it.

iew12q2.A: Correct. Modularity lets one platform serve varied customer needs, which raises satisfaction while keeping production efficient — Atomberg's modular attachment design is the course example.
iew12q2.B: Modularity generally improves scalability by reusing common parts.
iew12q2.C: Customisation increases customer engagement rather than reducing it.
iew12q2.D: Minimal options is the opposite of customisable.

iew12q3.A: Spreading resources thinly is precisely what a beachhead strategy avoids.
iew12q3.B: Correct. A beachhead is one focused segment you can win first, establishing a base before expanding — the reviewers' advice to 'get specific, narrow, choose one or two segments'.
iew12q3.C: It depends on customer research rather than skipping it.
iew12q3.D: It is an application of segmentation, not an avoidance of it.

iew12q4.A: Friends are the people the course tells founders not to rely on for feedback or reach.
iew12q4.B: Correct. Networking pays off when connections are targeted — reaching the specific customers, mentors and investors who matter to your venture.
iew12q4.C: Avoiding industry events removes the main venue for building a network.
iew12q4.D: Unstructured effort produces contacts but no outcomes.

iew12q5.A: Higher development costs are a disadvantage, never an advantage.
iew12q5.B: Correct. The inverted pyramid flips the usual hierarchy so the customer sits at the top, which forces the organisation to prioritise customer needs in its decisions.
iew12q5.C: Complex descriptions for a wider audience is the opposite of clarity.
iew12q5.D: This is the trap, and the most commonly chosen wrong answer. Concise messaging with a clear audience focus is the journalism sense of the inverted pyramid — most important information first — not the business model the course means.

iew12q6.A: Correct. Identifying the target customer segment is the step everything else depends on; get it wrong and the best-executed design still misses.
iew12q6.B: Ignoring user feedback is the failure mode, not a step.
iew12q6.C: Skipping competitor analysis to save time loses the market context.
iew12q6.D: Overlooking market research to focus on production builds the wrong thing efficiently.

iew12q7.A: Expensive extravagant campaigns are exactly what a cash-constrained startup cannot afford.
iew12q7.B: Short-term aggressive advertising buys attention without building anything durable.
iew12q7.C: Correct. Lean, innovative marketing fits a startup's budget and lets you test channels with small bets before committing.
iew12q7.D: Random, unfocused effort wastes the little budget there is.

iew12q8.A: Personal opinions substituted for user evidence is inventor syndrome.
iew12q8.B: Correct. Customer needs and preferences are the design input that matters — the single most repeated point in the whole course.
iew12q8.C: Excessive technical detail with low usability is over-engineering.
iew12q8.D: Low-impact trends chosen to reduce risk produce low-impact products.

iew12q9.A: Irrelevant features confuse the audience about what the product is for.
iew12q9.B: Overemphasising minor segments misrepresents the opportunity.
iew12q9.C: Correct. The solution slide must make clear exactly how the product addresses the specific problem you just established — the reviewers kept pressing teams on this.
iew12q9.D: Overambitious goals damage credibility with investors who have heard them before.

iew12q10.A: A vague concept is the fastest way to lose an investor's attention.
iew12q10.B: Avoiding market potential removes the thing investors most want to size.
iew12q10.C: Correct. Clearly articulating the value proposition and the market fit is the essential pitch element — any VC wants to understand how the business makes money.
iew12q10.D: Deliberately weak projections signal that you do not believe in the business.
